planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; unlike New England and New York asters, this Old World species resents heavy wet clay and winter waterlogging.

directions: Give this European species sharp drainage and a lean, chalky-to-average soil rather than the rich, moisture-retentive conditions that suit most fall asters; it sulks and rots in heavy wet ground. Its lavender-to-violet, yellow-centered daisies open earlier than most Michaelmas daisies, often from midsummer, extending the nectar season well before the New England aster rush begins. The compact, non-running clumps stay tidy without the aggressive spread of many native asters, making it a good fit for a small border or rock garden. Lift and divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to keep flowering strong.

common_name: King George Aster (Large Violet-Blue Italian Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; King George is a long-cultivated Italian aster selection introduced in 1914 and still grown for unusually large flowers on a compact plant.

directions: King George carries exceptionally large, single, violet-blue flowers with a bright gold eye, among the biggest blooms of any hardy aster, on stems that stay self-supporting without staking. It flowers earlier than the New England and New York asters, opening from late summer, and holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliability and flower quality over more than a century of cultivation. Give it lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich or waterlogged ground shortens its lifespan. Divide every two to three years in spring to renew vigor and preserve flower size.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this German-bred Italian aster selection ('Violet Queen') is prized for the deepest, most saturated flower color in the amellus group.

directions: Bred by the influential German nurseryman Karl Foerster, Violet Queen produces intensely saturated violet-purple, gold-centered daisies over a low, dense mound, the richest flower color found in the Italian aster group. Its compact, self-supporting habit and comparatively good resistance to the powdery mildew that plagues taller New York asters make it a dependable front-of-border choice. Provide lean, well-drained, full-sun conditions, since damp winter soil is its chief enemy rather than cold. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain a tight, floriferous habit.

common_name: September Ruby Aster (Deep Ruby-Red New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; September Ruby is a long-grown New England aster selection valued for the deepest red flower color in the species.

directions: September Ruby bears masses of glowing ruby-red, gold-centered daisies on sturdy, upright stems, standing out as one of the darkest, warmest-toned selections among the New England asters and a magnet for late-migrating monarchs and other pollinators. It carries the full cold hardiness and vigor of the wild species, tolerating heavier, moisture-retentive soils that would rot the more Mediterranean Italian asters. Pinch or shear stems back by about a third in early to midsummer to build a bushier, more self-supporting plant and delay bloom slightly for a fuller fall show. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower quality.

common_name: Woods Purple Aster (Compact Mildew-Resistant Purple New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Woods Purple completes the compact, mildew-resistant Woods series alongside Woods Blue and Woods Pink.

directions: Woods Purple forms the same tidy, dense mound as its Woods series siblings, but smothered in small, rich purple-violet, yellow-centered daisies rather than blue or pink, giving a deeper jewel-toned option for the front of a fall border. Like the rest of the series it shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than taller, older New York aster cultivars, staying presentable through a humid late season. Its low, compact habit needs no staking and suits mass planting or container use where larger asters would overwhelm the space. Pinch or shear back by a third in early summer to keep growth dense, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.
